courses.title: 1. MATLAB workflow and numerical thinking
courses.summary: Build a reproducible script, understand variables and floating-point numbers, and turn a calculation into a test.

lessons.title: Scripts, commands and a fresh workspace
paragraphs: MATLAB organizes work around arrays and named variables. A script is a sequence of statements saved in an .m file; running it executes those statements in order. Start with a question and units: for a 12 V supply across 6 ohms, current is voltage divided by resistance. Give inputs descriptive names so changing a parameter changes the calculation rather than a copied answer.

In desktop MATLAB the Command Window and Workspace help inspect results, while the Editor keeps a reproducible record. Here, edit the prepared script and press Run; each run begins with a fresh workspace. The browser uses a documented numeric subset. Download .m preserves your exact script for later use in MATLAB. Neither a license nor installation is needed for supported browser exercises.
lessons.pitfall: An old workspace variable can conceal a missing input in desktop MATLAB. Define all required inputs inside your experiment.

question.prompt: A reproducible script should obtain its input voltage from…

options.text: An unnamed variable left by yesterday’s session
An explicit assignment or documented input

question.explanation: Explicit inputs make the calculation repeatable and expose which assumption changed.

lessons.title: Assignment, output and comments
paragraphs: The equals sign assigns the value on its right to the name on its left. Names are case-sensitive: voltage and Voltage differ. A semicolon suppresses automatic display but does not stop computation. A percent sign begins a comment. Record why a number was chosen, and put units in variable names or comments because ordinary numeric arrays do not enforce physical dimensions.

Use disp(current_A) when output is part of the experiment. For voltage_V=12 and resistance_ohm=6, the expected current is 2 A and power is 24 W. Printing the current does not change it. Editing the voltage to 9 must produce 1.5 A and 13.5 W, which supplies a simple second test independent of the first numbers.
lessons.pitfall: Using = inside a comparison assigns in MATLAB syntax; use == when comparing values.

question.prompt: What does a trailing semicolon do?

options.text: Suppresses automatic display of that statement

question.explanation: The expression is still evaluated and stored; disp can show it explicitly.

lessons.title: Types, precision and units
paragraphs: Ordinary literals such as 12 and 0.1 create double-precision values in MATLAB. A logical condition represents true or false. Desktop MATLAB also offers integer types, single precision, complex numbers, text, tables and objects. This sandbox keeps finite real doubles, logical arrays, text labels and anonymous functions so unsupported types cannot silently change an exercise.

A double stores binary floating-point values. Many decimal fractions have no exact binary representation, so use an absolute tolerance for a known scale: abs(actual-expected)<1e-10. For measurements over many orders of magnitude combine an absolute and a relative tolerance. Keep unit conversion explicit: 250 milliamps is 0.25 amperes before multiplying by volts.
lessons.pitfall: Displayed digits are not a promise of exact arithmetic; exact == is unsuitable for many computed floating-point comparisons.

question.prompt: How should a calculated decimal be checked near a known value?

options.text: Compare its error with a justified tolerance
Require every printed decimal digit to match
Convert it to text before all arithmetic

question.explanation: Floating-point rounding requires a tolerance chosen for the scale and purpose of the result.

lessons.title: Assertions and a useful notebook
paragraphs: An assertion converts an expectation into an executable check. Write assert(abs(current_A-2)<1e-12) only when the input assumptions actually imply 2 A. Also check the domain before computing: resistance must be positive for this passive resistor example. A failed assertion is evidence to investigate, not a reason to remove the check.

Keep the script, a prediction and your observations together. This sandbox saves one notebook per preset in the current browser; export JSON to move it between devices. Loading and resetting ask before replacing work. Result exports identify the exact executed source, while a .m download contains the current editor text, including unfinished changes.
lessons.pitfall: A saved notebook is not proof that its code was executed; rerun after loading to generate new evidence.

question.prompt: What should an assertion express?

options.text: The exact answer currently shown, without reasoning

question.explanation: Assertions check independently justified expectations and fail when code violates them.

courses.title: 2. Vectors, matrices and indexing
courses.summary: Construct arrays, reason about shape, and select or update data using MATLAB’s one-based, column-major indexing.

lessons.title: Shape is part of the data
paragraphs: A scalar is a 1-by-1 array, a row vector is 1-by-N and a column vector is N-by-1. In [1 2; 3 4], spaces separate columns and a semicolon starts another row. Matrix dimensions describe a physical or mathematical meaning: rows might be time samples and columns might be sensors. Decide that convention before combining arrays.

zeros(m,n), ones(m,n) and eye(n) create known shapes. zeros(3) is 3-by-3, not a three-element row. Use size(A,1), size(A,2) and numel(A) to distinguish row count, column count and total elements. The sandbox rejects incompatible shapes; it implements scalar expansion but not desktop MATLAB’s general singleton expansion.
lessons.pitfall: A row vector and a column vector with the same values have different shapes and can produce very different expressions.

question.prompt: What shape does zeros(2,3) create?
question.explanation: The first argument sets rows and the second sets columns.

lessons.title: One-based indexing and column order
paragraphs: MATLAB indices start at one. A(2,1) means second row, first column. A single index walks down the first column before moving to the next: for A=[10 20;30 40], A(2)=30 and A(3)=20. This storage convention also determines the order of elements when reshaping or flattening an array.

A(:,2) selects the entire second column. A(1,end) selects the last column in row one; end is evaluated for its index position. A(:) returns a column containing all entries in column-major order. In the browser, indexed assignment modifies existing elements; initialize the full target with zeros first because automatic array growth is outside the subset.
lessons.pitfall: Index zero is invalid. A(3) does not mean row three when A has only two rows; it uses linear indexing.

question.explanation: Linear indices read [10;30;20;40], so the third element is 20.

lessons.title: Ranges, reshaping and transposes
paragraphs: The colon expression start:step:stop creates regularly spaced values while its two-argument form uses step one. A negative step creates descending values. linspace(a,b,n) chooses a count and includes both endpoints for n greater than one. These solve different tasks: a required sample interval and a required sample count should not be confused.

reshape(1:6,2,3) keeps the linear order, producing rows [1 3 5] and [2 4 6]. Transpose swaps row and column positions. Desktop apostrophe conjugates complex values, while dot-apostrophe does not; all browser values are real, so both have the same result here. Check shape and values after either transformation.
lessons.pitfall: reshape rearranges shape without sorting values; it cannot change the total number of elements.

question.prompt: What is the first row of reshape(1:6,2,3)?
question.explanation: Reshape fills columns first, preserving the original linear order.

lessons.title: Logical masks and updates
paragraphs: A comparison such as samples>3 returns logical values rather than positions. samples(samples>3) selects only entries for which the mask is true; find converts a logical selection into explicit one-based positions. Use a mask for a condition and a numeric index when the position itself is meaningful. Keep the original values if filtering is an analytical decision.

Try x=[1 4 2 8]. The mask x>3 selects [4 8], and x(x>3)=0 gives [1 0 2 0]. The sandbox requires a logical mask to match the indexed dimension exactly. It preserves logical type, so a numeric zero is not an alternative to false when used as a normal numeric index.
lessons.pitfall: Do not confuse logical masks with arrays of numeric zeros and ones: numeric zero is an invalid index.

question.prompt: Which expression selects values greater than 3 from x?
question.explanation: The comparison returns a logical mask that retains the matching entries.

courses.title: 3. Arithmetic and mathematical functions
courses.summary: Distinguish element-wise calculations from matrix operations, use trigonometric and exponential functions, and control numerical error.

lessons.title: Matrix and element-wise operators
paragraphs: The dot in .*, ./ and .^ changes the mathematical operation. If x=[1 2 3], x.^2 computes [1 4 9]. A*A combines rows and columns using dot products; A.*A squares corresponding entries. Both may be valid for a square matrix but answer different questions, so successful execution does not establish correctness.

For A=[1 2;3 4], A*A is [7 10;15 22] while A.*A is [1 4;9 16]. Predict one entry by hand before running. Multiplying a scalar by a matrix scales every entry. Equal-size arrays and scalar expansion are supported here; general singleton broadcasting remains a desktop MATLAB topic.
lessons.pitfall: A square array can hide a mistaken * because both operations produce outputs with the same dimensions.

question.prompt: Which expression squares each value in vector x?
question.explanation: The dot requests element-wise powers, independently for each entry.

lessons.title: Angles, logarithms and domains
paragraphs: sin, cos and tan use radians. sind, cosd and tand use degrees. Convert a full turn to 2*pi radians or use the degree functions consistently. exp(x) computes e to the power x, log is the natural logarithm, and log10 is the base-ten logarithm. A physical exponential needs a dimensionless exponent, such as time divided by a time constant.

For a decay y=exp(-t/tau), y is 1 at t=0 and approximately 0.367879 at t=tau. This browser rejects nonfinite and complex results: sqrt(-1) and log(0) stop with a domain explanation. Desktop MATLAB can represent complex numbers and Inf, so behavior outside the finite real domain intentionally differs.
lessons.pitfall: Mixing degrees and radians gives plausible but incorrect waveforms; write angle units in labels and variable names.

question.prompt: Which expression gives the sine of 30 degrees?
question.explanation: sind interprets its input in degrees, so the result is approximately 0.5.

lessons.title: Rounding, remainder and comparisons
paragraphs: floor rounds toward negative infinity, ceil toward positive infinity and fix toward zero. round uses nearest integer, with halfway cases away from zero. Compare floor(-1.7)=-2 with fix(-1.7)=-1. These choices matter for indexing bins, converting units and deciding when a threshold is crossed. Rounding is a modeling choice, not a repair for an unstable calculation.

mod and rem agree for many positive inputs but differ with signs. mod(-3,4)=1 follows floor-based division, while rem(-3,4)=-3 follows truncation. Boolean operators combine comparisons; use parentheses to make grouping visible. Scalar && and || short-circuit, so a guard can prevent evaluating an invalid expression such as division by zero.
lessons.pitfall: Applying floor when you mean truncation changes the handling of negative values.

question.prompt: What is mod(-3,4)?
question.explanation: Floor-based division chooses -1 times 4, leaving a remainder of 1.

lessons.title: Conditioning and error budgets
paragraphs: Two mathematically equivalent formulas need not have identical floating-point behavior. Subtracting nearly equal numbers can remove significant digits; multiplying extremely large values can overflow. Separate the sensitivity of the problem from the numerical stability of the algorithm. A stable algorithm cannot manufacture information missing from noisy measurements.

Check errors against reference cases over the relevant scale. For a sampled sine wave, abs(sin(t).^2+cos(t).^2-1) should remain small, but exact equality is unnecessary. Use max to reduce that error to a worst-case value and inspect the whole array if the check fails. State whether your tolerance is absolute, relative or both.
lessons.pitfall: Increasing the displayed precision cannot undo cancellation or inaccurate input measurements.

question.explanation: The identity is exact in real arithmetic, but numerical evaluations have small rounding errors.

courses.title: 4. Conditions, loops and reusable functions
courses.summary: Write control flow, preallocate results, build anonymous functions and test both ordinary and edge cases.

lessons.title: Decisions and scalar guards
paragraphs: if, elseif and else select a branch according to a condition; end closes the block. Think about equal values at every threshold. A temperature controller using T>30 should specify what happens at exactly 30. Mutually exclusive branches reduce ambiguity and make it easier to list expected behavior before writing the program.

Use scalar && or || for short-circuit guards. The expression resistance>0 && voltage/resistance<5 avoids division when resistance is zero. Element-wise & and | operate on arrays and do not supply that scalar short-circuit guarantee. In MATLAB, an array condition is true when it is nonempty and all entries are nonzero; prefer explicit all or any for clarity.
lessons.pitfall: Testing only values far from a threshold leaves equality and boundary behavior unverified.

question.prompt: Which operator can skip an unsafe right-hand scalar test?
question.explanation: Scalar && short-circuits when its left condition is false.

lessons.title: Loops and preallocation
paragraphs: A for loop visits the columns of its iteration array. The common for k=1:N uses a row vector, so each iteration receives one scalar index. Initialize y=zeros(1,N) and fill y(k) rather than changing the size every iteration. Preallocation exposes the intended shape and is required for indexed writes in this sandbox.

A while loop repeats while its condition remains true. Its body must make progress toward termination. Add an explicit iteration cap for iterative numerical methods because convergence is not guaranteed. break exits the nearest loop; continue advances to the next iteration. Browser operation and time limits stop accidental infinite loops without modifying a saved notebook.
lessons.pitfall: A column vector after for is one column, so it produces one vector-valued iteration rather than N scalar iterations.

question.prompt: Why preallocate y=zeros(1,N)?

options.text: It declares the full result shape before indexed writes
It makes all later calculations exact

question.explanation: Preallocation avoids repeated array growth and makes bounds explicit.

lessons.title: Anonymous and named functions
paragraphs: An anonymous function such as square=@(x) x.^2 wraps one expression behind a reusable interface. Call square([1 2 3]) to get [1 4 9]. Define which input shapes are supported; a function is more reusable when its assumptions are explicit. An anonymous function captures the values of external variables when it is created.

Desktop MATLAB also supports function files, local functions, multiple outputs and argument validation blocks. These are taught here with a separate desktop example, but the browser only executes anonymous functions. Prefer a named function for multiple statements and a clear testable contract. Avoid globals when inputs and outputs can carry the same information explicitly.
lessons.pitfall: Changing an outer scalar after creating an anonymous function does not retroactively update its captured value.

question.prompt: After a=2; f=@(x) a*x; a=3; what is f(4)?
question.explanation: The anonymous function captured a=2 when it was created.

lessons.title: Debugging through invariants
paragraphs: An invariant is a property that should remain true at a defined point in execution. In a running sum, after iteration k the accumulator should equal the sum of the first k terms. Small examples reveal whether the algorithm omits the first term, counts the last term twice or updates a value before it has been used.

Test no-work cases, a single iteration and representative larger inputs. Compare a loop result against an independently expressed vector calculation, while allowing a tolerance for noninteger data. In desktop MATLAB, breakpoints and the debugger reveal values at a failing line. Here, printed values, workspace inspection and line-numbered errors provide a compact debugging workflow.
lessons.pitfall: A test that repeats the same indexing mistake as the implementation is not an independent oracle.

courses.title: 5. Plotting and communicating results
courses.summary: Build meaningful plots with explicit coordinates, units and sampling, and inspect numerical evidence behind every curve.

lessons.title: Data coordinates and labels
paragraphs: A plot maps numeric coordinates to marks; it does not improve the quality of those numbers. plot(y) uses sample positions 1 through N for the horizontal axis, while plot(x,y) uses explicit x values. For a time series use a time vector in seconds and label both axes so the viewer can distinguish elapsed time from sample index.

The browser renders actual computed plot vectors and offers a sample inspector and numerical table. title, xlabel and ylabel describe the current axes. Desktop MATLAB offers figures, axes handles, tiledlayout, legends, annotations and many plot types. Those interfaces belong to the desktop reference unless their exact signatures appear as supported here.
lessons.pitfall: A line drawn against sample number cannot be interpreted as a line against seconds without a sampling interval.

question.prompt: Why prefer plot(t,y) for a sampled physical signal?

options.text: It converts volts into seconds automatically
It makes the actual time coordinates explicit

question.explanation: Explicit coordinates preserve the physical meaning of the horizontal axis.

lessons.title: Sampling and visible shape
paragraphs: A line plot joins the samples you supplied. A smooth-looking curve does not prove that the underlying signal is smooth or sufficiently sampled. Start with an expected timescale: a one-second sine period needs several samples per cycle to describe its shape. Increasing plotted resolution cannot recover information that was never measured.

For a synthetic signal, compare 9 points with 101 points over the same interval. Both include the endpoints with linspace, but the coarse polyline hides curvature. For measured data, keep the original samples and distinguish interpolation from new observations. The signal-processing course examines the stronger sampling requirements needed to avoid aliasing.
lessons.pitfall: A beautiful interpolated curve is not evidence that additional measurements exist.

question.prompt: What does a line between measured points establish?

options.text: That missing samples have been measured
That the true system followed exactly that line

question.explanation: The connector communicates a plotting convention; it does not create new measurements.

lessons.title: Comparisons on shared axes
paragraphs: Compare a model and a reference at the same time coordinates. In this sandbox hold("on") retains subsequent plot calls on the same axes and hold("off") restores replacement behavior. Each series has a numbered selector and exact data table, so the comparison is not dependent on distinguishing colors.

Plot a numerical approximation beside an analytical curve, then calculate the error separately. Curves can look identical when the axis range is large; max(abs(actual-reference)) exposes the largest difference. Conversely, a tight vertical range can exaggerate a physically unimportant discrepancy. Report both the numeric error and why that error is acceptable.
lessons.pitfall: Visual overlap alone does not prove accuracy; an explicit residual measures the difference.

question.prompt: Which numeric check supplements overlapping model and reference curves?
question.explanation: A maximum absolute residual quantifies the discrepancy that may be visually hidden.

lessons.title: Reusable figures and exported evidence
paragraphs: A useful figure includes the meaning of each axis, the units, the method and enough context to reproduce the data. Avoid hiding excluded observations. In desktop MATLAB, exportgraphics saves a figure at a chosen resolution or as a vector document. Keep the source data and script alongside that presentation artifact.

Here, export computed results to capture plot samples, printed output and the exact source. The plot inspector identifies one numeric sample at a time and the table paginates all samples. Workspace previews are bounded and labelled as previews; they must not be confused with a full numerical dataset. Editing the script removes previous results to prevent accidental attribution to new code.
lessons.pitfall: An image cannot reveal every value or prove which version of a script generated it.

question.explanation: The result file connects numerical samples to the exact script that generated them.

courses.title: 6. Linear systems and least squares
courses.summary: Solve Ax=b, verify residuals, fit an overdetermined system and understand when conditioning limits your conclusions.

lessons.title: From equations to matrix form
paragraphs: A matrix encodes coefficients of several equations. For 2*x+y=5 and x+3*y=7, set A=[2 1;1 3] and b=[5;7]. The vector b must have the same number of rows as A. Solving the equations gives x=1.6 and y=1.8; multiplying the result back by A reconstructs b.

Use A\b as the primary solve operation. Forming inv(A)*b adds an unnecessary inverse and can worsen numerical behavior. The browser uses a bounded pivoted elimination for square matrices and a small QR-based least-squares path for tall full-rank systems. It rejects singular or severely ill-conditioned inputs rather than inventing a solution.
lessons.pitfall: Matrix division is an equation solve, not independent division of corresponding entries.

question.prompt: Which expression directly solves A*x=b?
question.explanation: Backslash solves the linear system using the coefficient matrix and right-hand side.

lessons.title: Residuals and sensitivity
paragraphs: The residual r=A*x-b measures how well the computed vector satisfies the supplied equations. Its size should be interpreted relative to the scale of A, x and b. A small residual is necessary evidence, but it does not guarantee a small error in x when the system is sensitive to small changes in its data.

Consider nearly dependent rows: two measurements that convey almost the same equation provide little independent information. Small measurement noise can then cause a large solution change. Desktop cond and rcond help investigate conditioning; svd reveals directions with weak information. None of those desktop diagnostics is replaced by the browser’s simple singularity threshold.
lessons.pitfall: A tiny residual does not establish that a poorly conditioned solution is physically reliable.

question.prompt: What can a small residual fail to guarantee?

options.text: That the code computed a residual
A small solution error in an ill-conditioned problem
That A*x is close to b

question.explanation: Sensitivity can amplify tiny coefficient or data errors even when the supplied equations are satisfied closely.

lessons.title: Overdetermined measurements
paragraphs: A tall matrix has more equations than unknowns. No single vector may satisfy every noisy measurement, so least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals. To fit y=m*t+c, use a column of times and a column of ones. The two fitted coefficients have different units: slope is output per time and intercept has output units.

For t=[0;1;2] and y=[1;3;5], A=[t ones(3,1)] and A\y return [2;1]. Add noise to one observation and inspect how residuals distribute. A nonzero residual is expected for inconsistent data. QR factorization avoids explicitly forming the normal equations, which can square the condition number.
lessons.pitfall: Do not demand a zero residual from an intentionally noisy overdetermined system.

question.prompt: What does a least-squares fit minimize?

options.text: Every individual residual independently to zero

question.explanation: The objective is a single aggregate squared-error measure across all observations.

lessons.title: Factorizations and numerical checks
paragraphs: LU, QR and SVD are different decompositions with different uses. LU supports many square solves; QR supports least squares; SVD reveals rank and helps with minimum-norm problems. Eigenvalues characterize square linear transformations and dynamical systems. A determinant is useful in small analytical examples but is a poor standalone numerical conditioning test.

For a desktop investigation, compare a solve against a known manufactured solution: choose x_true, construct b=A*x_true, solve and measure error. Then perturb b slightly and compare the resulting change. Test multiple scales and include a singular example. The browser supports small full-rank systems; specialized sparse, rank-deficient and eigenvalue workflows use desktop functions.
lessons.pitfall: A nonzero determinant in finite precision does not imply that solving the matrix is numerically safe.

question.prompt: Which factorization is especially useful for studying numerical rank?
question.explanation: Singular values quantify independent directions and expose near-dependence.

courses.expected: x=[1.6;1.8], fit=[2;1], and the square-system residual is near zero. The tall system recovers the slope and intercept of y=2*t+1.

courses.title: 7. Data, statistics and import workflows
courses.summary: Summarize measurements, distinguish sample and population statistics, and design a defensible data-cleaning workflow.

lessons.title: Observations, variables and units
paragraphs: A dataset needs a schema before it needs a formula. State what one row represents, which unit each column uses and whether the observations are independent. A sensor matrix with time down rows and devices across columns has a different meaning from a matrix of repeated laboratory runs. Numeric arrays are convenient when every entry shares a meaningful numeric interpretation.

Desktop MATLAB tables attach names to heterogeneous variables; timetables additionally organize observations by time. readtable, readmatrix and detectImportOptions help import files. This browser lab uses explicit numeric fixtures instead of reading host files. Preserve an original copy of measurements before cleaning, and record each transformation as code rather than manual editing.
lessons.pitfall: A column name cannot repair mixed units; convert units before combining measurements.

question.prompt: What should be specified before summarizing a dataset?

options.text: What each row and column means, including units

question.explanation: A defined schema prevents calculations on incompatible quantities.

lessons.title: Center, spread and normalization
paragraphs: mean measures an arithmetic center, while median uses the middle of sorted observations and resists isolated extremes. Standard deviation measures spread about the mean. std(x) uses sample normalization by N-1 for ordinary vectors; std(x,1) uses population normalization by N. Neither number describes causation or guarantees a normal distribution.

For [1 2 3], the mean and median are 2, sample variance is 1 and population variance is 2/3. Add a large outlier and compare the mean with the median. For a matrix, reductions default to the first nonsingleton dimension; use an explicit dimension when your row/column convention makes that intent clearer.
lessons.pitfall: Standard deviation and standard error are different: the latter concerns uncertainty in an estimated mean under additional assumptions.

question.prompt: What is var([1 2 3]) with sample normalization?
question.explanation: Squared deviations sum to 2, and division by N-1=2 gives 1.

lessons.title: Missing data and exclusions
paragraphs: A missing value is not automatically a physical zero. In desktop MATLAB, missing representations depend on type, such as NaN in numeric arrays and NaT in dates. ismissing, rmmissing and fillmissing support explicit policies. Choose a policy based on the measurement process; deleting inconvenient values can bias your conclusion.

The browser accepts finite values, so this exercise keeps validity as a separate logical mask. For values=[10 999 12 11] and valid=[true false true true], summarize values(valid) and record that one sample was excluded. The mask is evidence of a stated rule, not permission to remove every large observation. Compare the result with and without the suspect value.
lessons.pitfall: Replacing missing measurements with zero changes both the mean and the meaning of the dataset.

question.prompt: How should a missing temperature be handled?

options.text: Apply and document a justified missing-data policy
Always replace it with zero degrees
Delete it without recording the count

question.explanation: A policy needs to reflect why the value is missing and how exclusions affect the analysis.

lessons.title: Validation before conclusions
paragraphs: Summary statistics can conceal a failed sensor or a mixed population. Plot measurements against time and inspect ranges, counts and units. Check whether grouping or filtering changes which population you describe. A precise mean from an incorrectly calibrated instrument is still inaccurate. Measurements require both numeric checks and knowledge of how data were collected.

Build a small reference dataset whose statistics can be calculated by hand, then test the same analysis on the intended measurements. Report the original count, retained count, exclusion rule and chosen normalization. In desktop work, preserve import options and file provenance. Browser notebooks preserve code and notes, allowing the same analytical choices to be reviewed later.
lessons.pitfall: Statistical precision is not the same as measurement accuracy or unbiased sampling.

courses.title: 8. Interpolation, regression and polynomials
courses.summary: Estimate values between samples, fit a trend, and use residuals and held-out observations to challenge a model.

lessons.title: Interpolation between known samples
paragraphs: Interpolation constructs a value between observed coordinates. Linear interpolation uses the two neighboring points: at the midpoint between x=0,y=1 and x=2,y=5, it returns y=3. It honors the supplied samples exactly, which is useful for a lookup table but can also preserve every error in noisy measurements.

Use interp1(x,y,xq) with strictly increasing x values in the browser. Queries must remain within the known interval; extrapolation is rejected rather than assigned a plausible value. Desktop MATLAB offers additional methods, shapes and extrapolation controls. A method should reflect the smoothness, monotonicity and physical constraints of the actual problem.
lessons.pitfall: An interpolated value is an estimate derived from samples, not an additional independent observation.

question.prompt: Linear interpolation halfway between (0,1) and (2,5) gives…
question.explanation: The halfway position takes halfway of the output change: 1+(5-1)/2=3.

lessons.title: Regression and residuals
paragraphs: Regression estimates a relationship without requiring it to pass through every observation. polyfit(x,y,d) fits polynomial coefficients in descending powers, while polyval evaluates those coefficients. A degree-one fit has coefficients [slope intercept]. Use the model to express a hypothesis, not to decorate arbitrary data with a smooth line.

For x=[0 1 2 3] and y=[1 3 5 7], a linear fit returns approximately [2 1]. Perturb one observation and inspect y-polyval(p,x). Residual patterns suggest omitted structure; random-looking residuals alone do not prove the model is correct. Track the units of every coefficient and check whether an intercept has a physical interpretation.
lessons.pitfall: Confusing descending polynomial coefficient order changes the model while leaving the code syntactically valid.

question.prompt: What model do coefficients [2 1] represent?
question.explanation: polyval interprets the first coefficient as the highest power, here the slope.

lessons.title: Degree, scaling and overfitting
paragraphs: A higher-degree polynomial has more flexibility, which can fit noise and behave badly outside the observed interval. More coefficients do not guarantee better predictions. Compare model choices on held-out observations that were not used to determine their coefficients. The split must respect time or group structure when random splitting would leak information.

Polynomial basis columns can become poorly scaled when x is large or the degree is high. Centering and scaling x can improve numerical behavior, but the transformation must also be applied to future queries. The browser caps degree at six and uses a small full-rank least-squares solver; desktop polyfit offers richer diagnostics and scaling outputs.
lessons.pitfall: Selecting degree using only training error favors unnecessary complexity and can hide worse prediction error.

question.prompt: Which evidence helps select polynomial degree?

options.text: The number of digits in the coefficients

question.explanation: Held-out evaluation challenges whether fitted structure generalizes beyond the fitting samples.

lessons.title: Calibration as an engineering task
paragraphs: A calibration maps a measured signal into an estimated physical quantity. Define the calibration range, uncertainty and reference measurement process. Fitting voltage to temperature requires accurate reference temperatures, not just a convenient sequence of numbers. A fit with a small residual can still be wrong outside its measured range.

Create a synthetic calibration with known coefficients, recover them and test a query inside the range. Then add noise or an outlier and observe the change. Document whether your result is interpolation or regression and whether an extrapolated query is permitted. Export the script and parameters so later measurements use the same model and units.

courses.title: 9. Numerical differentiation, integration and roots
courses.summary: Approximate derivatives and integrals from samples, refine resolution and solve scalar equations with bracketed roots.

lessons.title: Differences and physical derivatives
paragraphs: diff(y) subtracts neighboring samples; it is not automatically a derivative. Divide by the corresponding spacing in x to obtain a slope. For equally spaced samples, gradient(y,h) uses centered differences in the interior and one-sided differences at boundaries. Those boundary formulas have different accuracy and deserve separate inspection.

If position is measured in meters and time in seconds, the derivative has units of meters per second. For y=t.^2, the analytical derivative is 2*t. Compare the interior values first, then the endpoints. Differentiation can amplify measurement noise because a small spacing divides an already uncertain difference.
lessons.pitfall: Shrinking a finite-difference step indefinitely can increase rounding and noise errors instead of improving accuracy.

question.prompt: What additional quantity does diff(position) need to become velocity?
question.explanation: Velocity divides position differences by elapsed time.

lessons.title: Integrating sampled data
paragraphs: trapz(x,y) adds trapezoids between sample coordinates. Each area is the coordinate width times the average of its endpoint heights. This works on nonuniform spacing when x values are provided. Omitting x assumes unit spacing, which changes the physical result if your real sample interval is not one.

For y=t.^2 from 0 to 1, the exact integral is 1/3. A trapezoidal estimate on 101 equally spaced points is 0.33335, about 1.6667e-5 high. Halving the spacing reduces the smooth-function trapezoidal error by roughly a factor of four. Desktop integral evaluates a function adaptively; sampled-data integration cannot request new measurements.
lessons.pitfall: trapz(y) silently assumes unit spacing; always provide physical coordinates when spacing matters.

question.prompt: Why does trapz(t,y) matter when samples are 0.01 seconds apart?

options.text: It includes the actual time spacing
It automatically changes y to a symbolic expression

question.explanation: The coordinate widths determine the area and its physical units.

lessons.title: Bracketing a root
paragraphs: A root satisfies f(x)=0. A continuous function with opposite signs at interval endpoints has at least one root inside. Bisection repeatedly chooses the half interval that retains a sign change. It is slower than some advanced methods but exposes the assumptions and offers a predictable reduction in bracket width.

The browser fzero subset accepts an anonymous scalar function and a two-point sign-changing bracket. It uses bounded bisection, not the full MATLAB implementation. For f=@(x) x.^2-2 on [0 2], the root is approximately 1.41421356. Check the residual and explain the bracket; a discontinuity can produce a sign change without a true root.
lessons.pitfall: A sign change only guarantees a root when the function is continuous on the bracket.

lessons.title: Convergence and numerical evidence
paragraphs: A single numerical answer says little about its discretization error. Repeat an integration with successively finer grids and compare against an analytical case when possible. Keep data error, approximation error and floating-point rounding conceptually separate. A grid study may reveal that the chosen method has not reached its expected convergence behavior.

State the quantity being checked, its units and the acceptance tolerance. For a root, inspect both the residual and bracket width because a flat or steep function changes their relationship. For a derivative, compare interior and endpoint errors separately. Record the refinement table in your notebook instead of accepting an attractive plot as the only evidence.
lessons.pitfall: Agreement between two coarse approximations is not proof of convergence or correctness.

courses.title: 10. Differential equations and physical simulation
courses.summary: Turn a rate law into a time simulation, test stability and convergence, and connect explicit steps to desktop ODE solvers.

lessons.title: States, rates and initial conditions
paragraphs: A differential equation describes a rate of change, not the state directly. A first-order decay obeys dy/dt=-y/tau with initial condition y(0)=1. Its analytical solution is exp(-t/tau). Units must agree: if time is seconds, tau is seconds and dy/dt has state units per second. The initial condition selects one trajectory from a family of possible solutions.

Choose a state vector that contains enough information to compute the next rate. A mass-spring system needs position and velocity; specifying only position leaves its future ambiguous. The browser example starts with a scalar decay so you can compare every time sample with an exact solution before expanding to multiple coupled states.
lessons.pitfall: An equation without an initial condition does not define a unique simulation trajectory.

question.prompt: What extra information selects a decay trajectory?
question.explanation: The initial condition fixes which solution of the differential equation is being followed.

lessons.title: Forward Euler as an explicit recurrence
paragraphs: Forward Euler estimates the next state as y_next=y+h*f(t,y). For decay this becomes y_next=y*(1-h/tau). This recurrence is an approximation to the differential equation; making the plot smooth does not change the method. Calculate its first update by hand to establish that the code implements the intended rate law.

For tau=1 and h=0.1, the first value is 0.9 instead of exp(-0.1)≈0.904837. The time vector and state arrays must share the same sample count, and the update loop stops one index before the end. Preallocate the output and store each state before advancing so the x and y coordinates remain aligned.
lessons.pitfall: An off-by-one loop can label y at t+h with t, producing a convincing but time-shifted plot.

question.prompt: For y=1, tau=1 and h=0.1, what is one Euler step?
question.explanation: The rate is -1, so y_next=1+0.1*(-1)=0.9.

lessons.title: Stability and step refinement
paragraphs: For this decay equation, Euler’s amplification factor is 1-h/tau. Magnitude below one gives asymptotic decay, while a negative factor creates alternating signs. Thus 0<h/tau<2 is the linear stability interval, and 0<h/tau<=1 additionally avoids sign oscillation for a positive initial state. Stability is not the same as sufficient accuracy.

Run the same final time with h=0.1, 0.05 and 0.025. Compare the maximum error to the analytical curve and the error at a fixed final time. Euler’s global error is first order under suitable smoothness conditions, so halving h should roughly halve error once you are in the convergence regime. Stiff systems can force very small explicit steps.
lessons.pitfall: A bounded-looking numerical trajectory can still be too inaccurate for its intended use.

question.prompt: Which h/tau is outside Euler’s asymptotic stability interval for decay?
question.explanation: The factor 1-2.5=-1.5 has magnitude greater than one and grows in magnitude.

lessons.title: Desktop solvers and model limits
paragraphs: Desktop ode45 solves many nonstiff initial-value problems using adaptive Runge-Kutta stepping; ode15s is an option for stiff problems. The derivative function receives t and y and returns rates of the matching state dimension. Solver tolerances control numerical error estimates, not uncertainty in a physical model or sensor data.

The desktop companion uses ode45 and compares with the same analytical decay. It is not executed in this browser. For any solver, check units, state ordering, initial conditions, events and a reference case. A successful numerical solve establishes behavior of the supplied equations, not that those equations accurately represent a real device.
lessons.pitfall: Tightening solver tolerances cannot fix an incorrect rate law or an uncalibrated physical parameter.

courses.title: 11. Sampling, convolution and frequency analysis
courses.summary: Generate sampled signals, implement a finite impulse response filter and understand desktop FFT workflows and their limits.

lessons.title: Sample rate and aliasing
paragraphs: Sampling converts a continuous-time signal into values at discrete instants. A sample rate Fs gives spacing 1/Fs seconds. A sinusoid at frequency f can be written sin(2*pi*f*t). Frequencies separated by multiples of the sample rate can produce indistinguishable sample patterns; this is aliasing, not a plotting defect.

For an appropriately band-limited signal, the sample rate must exceed twice the highest represented frequency to avoid idealized aliasing. Real acquisition also needs anti-alias filtering before sampling. Try generating frequencies on either side of Fs/2 and inspect the sampled values. Interpolating those samples afterward cannot undo arbitrary aliasing.
lessons.pitfall: The highest visible wiggle in a sampled plot is not necessarily the original analog frequency.

question.prompt: At Fs=100 Hz, what is the Nyquist frequency?
question.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate; acquisition needs appropriate band limitation.

lessons.title: Convolution and finite filters
paragraphs: A finite impulse response filter combines nearby samples with a fixed set of coefficients. Convolution sums products of shifted inputs and coefficients. A moving average with M entries uses coefficients ones(1,M)/M, giving unity gain for constant input once the window is filled. The full convolution has N+M-1 entries for lengths N and M.

The browser conv function returns full convolution. To compare a causal filter with N input samples, inspect the first N outputs and recognize startup transients from zero-valued samples before the beginning. Do not remove that transient without documenting the boundary assumption. A smoother curve can also have delayed features and attenuated peaks.
lessons.pitfall: Smoothing changes timing and amplitude; it is not a free improvement to every signal.

question.prompt: What length does full convolution of lengths 5 and 3 have?
question.explanation: The full output spans N+M-1=7 positions.

lessons.title: FFT bins, scaling and leakage
paragraphs: The discrete Fourier transform expresses a finite sample sequence in complex sinusoidal components. Desktop fft computes it efficiently. For N uniformly spaced samples, frequency-bin spacing is Fs/N. A real-valued signal produces conjugate symmetry; constructing a single-sided amplitude spectrum requires deliberate normalization and treatment of DC and the Nyquist bin.

A finite record implicitly repeats in the transform. If its ends do not connect smoothly, energy spreads across bins, often called spectral leakage. Windows change that tradeoff and their amplitude scaling must be accounted for. The browser teaches filtering with real arrays; complex FFT execution is a desktop feature, never simulated by an unrelated magnitude formula.
lessons.pitfall: Zero-padding gives denser displayed frequency samples but does not create a longer measurement record or new resolving power.

question.prompt: What is FFT bin spacing for Fs=100 and N=200?
question.explanation: The spacing is Fs/N, which equals 0.5 hertz.

lessons.title: Filter verification
paragraphs: Start with test signals whose behavior is known. A unit impulse should reproduce the filter coefficients. A constant signal should approach the sum of those coefficients after startup. A mixed slow and fast sinusoid reveals which frequencies are reduced, while a step exposes delay and settling. Validate more than one property before calling a filter useful.

In desktop MATLAB, filter applies numerator/denominator difference equations and Signal Processing Toolbox adds frequency-response and design tools such as freqz and butter. Keep base MATLAB and toolbox requirements visible. The browser notebook computes a moving-average result from actual convolution; it does not claim a production filter design or real sensor acquisition.
lessons.pitfall: Reducing a noisy-looking waveform does not prove the desired information was preserved.

question.explanation: By convolution, a unit impulse reproduces the impulse response coefficients.

courses.title: 12. Control systems and Simulink concepts
courses.summary: Build an explicit feedback simulation, reason about saturation and connect equations to desktop control and block-diagram tools.

lessons.title: Plant, reference and error
paragraphs: A feedback loop compares a measured output with a desired reference, computes an error and chooses an input to a plant. Define the signs carefully: error=reference-output supports negative feedback when a positive control input raises the output. Sensors, actuators and computation all introduce limitations that are absent from a bare equation.

The teaching plant follows dy/dt=-y+u with a one-second time constant and unit steady gain. A proportional controller uses u=Kp*(r-y). For r=1 and Kp=2 without saturation, the equilibrium is y=2/3, not 1. The remaining steady error is a property of this controller and plant, not automatically a coding bug.
lessons.pitfall: The sign of feedback matters: reversing the error can amplify deviations instead of correcting them.

question.prompt: For this plant with Kp=2 and r=1, what is the unsaturated equilibrium?
question.explanation: At equilibrium y=u=2*(1-y), so 3*y=2.

lessons.title: Discrete updates and saturation
paragraphs: A digital simulation updates state at discrete intervals. Compute the controller from the current measured state, clamp it to the actuator’s permitted range, then advance the plant with the chosen numerical method. Keep the clamp visible because it changes the system from the unconstrained linear equations used in many hand calculations.

Use min(max(u,lower),upper) for scalar saturation. In this course the actuator can supply from 0 to 2 model units. A large reference may remain unreachable even with a higher gain. Test both a small unsaturated command and a command that reaches the limit. The browser simulation uses Euler steps and inherits the numerical method’s stability and accuracy limits.
lessons.pitfall: A saturated actuator cannot implement the unbounded command computed by a mathematical controller.

question.prompt: Why clamp a simulated actuator command?

options.text: To represent its defined output limits
To prove the physical hardware is safe

question.explanation: The clamp is a model of limited actuation, not a guarantee about a real device.

lessons.title: Integral action and windup
paragraphs: Integral action accumulates error and can remove a constant steady error when the plant and controller permit it. A discrete integral update includes the sample interval: integral=integral+h*error. Omitting h makes controller behavior change unpredictably when you change the simulation rate. Derivative action is sensitive to measurement noise and requires careful implementation.

If an actuator is saturated while the integrator keeps growing, the accumulated command may remain excessive after the error changes sign. This is integral windup. Anti-windup policies include conditional integration and feedback of the saturation difference. Implement and compare a policy explicitly; merely naming a controller PID does not supply those details.
lessons.pitfall: An integral sum without the time-step factor is not a consistent approximation to a time integral.

courses.title: 13. Random experiments and Monte Carlo
courses.summary: Create reproducible random experiments, estimate uncertainty and distinguish sampling error from incorrect model assumptions.

lessons.title: Random distributions and seeds
paragraphs: rand generates uniform samples between zero and one, while randn generates approximately standard-normal samples. Scaling and shifting change their units and parameters: mu+sigma*randn(1,N) models independent normal measurements with specified mean and standard deviation. The choice of distribution is an assumption to justify, not a convenience that guarantees realism.

A pseudorandom generator evolves deterministic state. rng(seed) makes a run repeatable within a specified implementation. This browser uses its own documented teaching generator, so seed 42 does not produce MATLAB’s seed-42 sequence. Compare distributions and analytical properties across environments rather than expecting identical values from different generators.
lessons.pitfall: A seed guarantees reproducibility for the specified generator, not that a distribution accurately represents reality.

question.prompt: What does the browser rng seed guarantee?

options.text: The same sequence as MATLAB’s default generator

question.explanation: The algorithm and seed together determine the sequence; different generators can differ.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo estimation
paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimates a quantity by averaging results over sampled inputs. To estimate pi, sample independent x and y uniformly in the unit square and count points satisfying x^2+y^2<=1. The quarter-circle occupies pi/4 of the square, so four times the observed fraction estimates pi. The geometrical argument gives an independent reference.

Write the indicator as a logical array and take its mean. Report the number of samples and seed, then repeat with a different seed. Results vary because a finite random sample is not the entire population. Avoid selecting the most favorable run: choosing the run closest to pi understates the variability of the method.
lessons.pitfall: One lucky estimate near the reference is not evidence that every small-sample run is accurate.

question.prompt: Why multiply the accepted fraction by four in this pi estimate?

options.text: Because rand always generates four columns
A quarter-circle of radius one has area pi/4
Because every random variable has four states

question.explanation: The unit square has area one, so the geometric probability is pi/4.

lessons.title: Uncertainty and sample size
paragraphs: For independent Bernoulli observations with probability p, the sample proportion has standard deviation approximately sqrt(p*(1-p)/N). A plug-in estimate uses the observed proportion. Multiplying the proportion by four also multiplies its standard error by four. This describes sampling variability under the assumed independent model, not every possible source of error.

Monte Carlo error often shrinks like 1/sqrt(N), so reducing the typical error by a factor of two requires roughly four times as many samples. More samples cannot repair biased sampling or a wrong distribution. When events are rare, a run with no events may still be compatible with a nonzero probability; interpret uncertainty rather than reporting certainty.
lessons.pitfall: Doubling sample size does not generally halve Monte Carlo standard error.

question.prompt: How many samples are typically needed to halve Monte Carlo standard error?

options.text: The same number with a different title

question.explanation: The 1/sqrt(N) scaling means a factor of four in N produces a factor of two in standard error.

lessons.title: Verification and reproducible reports
paragraphs: Test the mechanics separately from the probabilistic outcome. A fixed seed should repeat exactly within this environment; every uniform sample should lie in [0,1), and accepted counts must be between zero and N. Those are deterministic invariants. Proximity to pi is a probabilistic result and should not be asserted with an unrealistically tiny tolerance.

For a report, preserve seed, distribution, sample count, estimator and uncertainty calculation. Repeat across several seeds and compare the variation with the predicted standard error. In desktop parallel work, manage independent random streams explicitly; resetting the same seed in every worker can duplicate samples. The next computing course discusses independent tasks and data movement.
lessons.pitfall: Giving every parallel task an identical seeded stream can create duplicates rather than independent evidence.

options.text: Every estimate equals pi to twelve digits

question.explanation: The range is guaranteed by the generator contract, while estimator error is random.

courses.title: 14. Optimization and parameter estimation
courses.summary: Define an objective, explore a bounded search, validate a fitted parameter and understand local versus global numerical results.

lessons.title: Objectives, variables and constraints
paragraphs: Optimization chooses decision variables to minimize or maximize an objective. Start by writing its units, permissible domain and meaning. Fitting a decay time constant can minimize the sum of squared differences between predicted and observed outputs, with tau constrained positive. Constraints represent allowed choices; they are not merely instructions for a solver.

For y(t)=exp(-t/tau), a candidate tau generates a complete predicted curve. Sum the squared residuals at the actual observation times. Comparing predictions to a differently sampled or shifted sequence would optimize the wrong objective. Keep measurement uncertainty and any weighting assumptions visible; squared error gives large residuals disproportionate influence.
lessons.pitfall: A solver can efficiently optimize a badly specified objective and still produce an unhelpful answer.

question.prompt: What should be defined before choosing an optimizer?
question.explanation: Those definitions establish the mathematical problem that a numerical method will solve.

lessons.title: Grid search as a transparent baseline
paragraphs: A bounded grid search evaluates the objective at a known set of candidates and retains the best. It is easy to inspect and makes a useful baseline for a one-dimensional problem. The winner is best among those candidates, not necessarily the exact continuous optimum. Finer spacing improves resolution at additional cost.

Search tau from 0.5 to 2.5 in steps of 0.05. If the synthetic observations use tau=1.5, the exact parameter is on the grid and should minimize error near zero. Change the true value to 1.53 and observe the resolution limit. A minimum at the boundary may indicate that your search range excludes a better solution.
lessons.pitfall: Calling a grid winner the global continuous optimum overstates what was actually searched.

question.prompt: What does a grid search establish?

options.text: That the model is physically correct
The best objective among evaluated candidates
The exact optimum over every real number

question.explanation: Only the finite candidate set has been evaluated directly.

lessons.title: Local methods and derivatives
paragraphs: Desktop fminsearch offers derivative-free local minimization, while fminbnd addresses a bounded scalar problem. Optimization Toolbox adds constrained and least-squares solvers such as fmincon and lsqnonlin. Different methods assume different structure; smoothness, scaling and constraints influence whether a method makes reliable progress.

A local optimum is better than nearby choices but may not be the best over the whole domain. Try several initial points where multiple basins are possible, and inspect convergence information. Derivatives can accelerate methods but incorrect gradients can mislead them. Compare an analytical gradient against finite differences at representative points before trusting it.
lessons.pitfall: A solver’s success flag is not a proof of global optimality or a correct physical model.

question.prompt: What can a local optimizer miss?

options.text: A better solution in another region

question.explanation: Local search need not explore distant basins of attraction.

lessons.title: Identifiability and validation
paragraphs: A fitted parameter is identifiable only when the observations constrain it sufficiently. If every observation occurs near t=0, many decay constants may produce nearly indistinguishable predictions. Low residuals can therefore coexist with uncertain parameters. Examine how the objective changes around the fitted value and collect data that excite informative dynamics.

Keep some observations separate from fitting and compare predictions on them. Recover a known parameter from synthetic data first, then add controlled noise to study sensitivity. Report the search range, resolution or solver settings, residual metric and limitations. A parameter estimate should carry enough context for another learner to reproduce and challenge it.
lessons.pitfall: A low training error does not guarantee parameter identifiability or predictive accuracy.

question.explanation: The observations may not distinguish different parameter choices strongly enough.

courses.expected: The minimum is at tau=1.5 with nearly zero loss because the synthetic observations use that value and it lies on the search grid. The curve makes the finite search range visible.

courses.title: 15. Performance, vectorization and memory
courses.summary: Preserve correctness while changing data access, preallocation and algorithm structure, then design a fair desktop benchmark.

lessons.title: Correctness before speed
paragraphs: A faster result is useful only if it answers the same problem to an acceptable accuracy. Establish a reference output, input domain and error tolerance before changing implementation. Integer examples can admit exact checks; floating-point reductions may differ slightly when operations are regrouped. Keep those differences separate from outright missing elements or changed equations.

The browser exercise compares a loop for a*x+b with an element-wise vector expression. Both compute actual outputs, but the browser does not measure MATLAB throughput or emulate its JIT compiler. Use this local experiment to verify equivalence and shape. Measure native performance in MATLAB using the desktop companion after checking correctness.
lessons.pitfall: Browser operation counts or JavaScript timings are not MATLAB benchmark results.

question.prompt: What is the first requirement of a performance optimization?

options.text: Reduce line count at any cost
Preserve the intended result and accepted error

question.explanation: Performance is meaningful only for an equivalent, validated computation.

lessons.title: Preallocation and vector expressions
paragraphs: Preallocation creates the final storage shape before a loop writes results. Vectorization expresses operations over arrays, allowing MATLAB to use optimized numerical kernels where applicable. It often simplifies intent, but can also create large temporary arrays. Compare the memory requirements of the complete expression, not only the visible input and output.

For x=1:N, y=3*x+2 expresses the same map as a loop. A pairwise difference matrix between N points, however, requires N squared entries. At N=10000 that is 100 million doubles, about 800 million bytes before temporary arrays. A blocked algorithm can reduce peak memory even if its source contains loops.
lessons.pitfall: Vectorizing an algorithm can increase memory use enough to outweigh reduced interpreter overhead.

question.prompt: How many entries are in a dense N-by-N pairwise array?
question.explanation: Both dimensions scale with N, so storage grows quadratically.

lessons.title: Timing and profiling in desktop MATLAB
paragraphs: timeit repeatedly measures a function and returns a timing estimate; tic/toc can measure a chosen interval. Define whether setup, allocation, transfers and output are inside that interval. Warm-up, background load and problem size affect observations. Use multiple sizes and preserve outputs so the benchmark still represents the real task.

The profiler identifies where time is spent, but instrumentation can change timings. Use profiling to choose a target, then run separate measurements to evaluate the improvement. Report MATLAB release, hardware, input size and the statistic used. A microbenchmark of a tiny vector may be dominated by call overhead rather than arithmetic throughput.
lessons.pitfall: Timing one run and reporting many decimal places gives a false impression of certainty.

question.prompt: What should a benchmark report besides elapsed time?
question.explanation: Those details determine what work the measurement actually represents.

lessons.title: Complexity, locality and bottlenecks
paragraphs: Algorithmic complexity describes how work grows with input size; locality describes how that work accesses memory. A dense matrix product grows roughly cubically in its dimension, while a simple element-wise map grows linearly in element count. Data that exceed cache can shift a workload from arithmetic-limited to memory-limited behavior.

MATLAB arrays use column-major storage, so consecutive elements down a column are contiguous. However, the execution engine and library calls can transform a high-level operation. Do not infer exact cache events from source order alone. Consider sparse storage when the problem structure warrants it, and validate results across sizes before interpreting any observed scaling curve.
lessons.pitfall: A smaller asymptotic complexity does not predict every crossover point for small real workloads.

question.prompt: Which entries are adjacent in MATLAB’s column-major layout?
question.explanation: Linear storage proceeds down a column before moving to the next.

courses.title: 16. Parallel computing, GPUs and scaling
courses.summary: Recognize independent work, reason about data movement and scaling limits, and prepare verified MATLAB parallel and GPU experiments.

lessons.title: Independent tasks and parfor
paragraphs: Parallel work must have a valid dependency structure. Independent parameter trials can run in any order if each writes its own output slot. A recurrence in which iteration k+1 reads the result of k cannot be changed to parfor without changing the algorithm. Dependencies matter more than the visual presence of a for loop.

Desktop Parallel Computing Toolbox provides workers and parfor. Classifying loop variables as sliced outputs, broadcasts, temporaries or reductions helps explain what information crosses tasks. The browser executes ordinary bounded loops; it does not start MATLAB workers or report parallel speedups. Its parameter-sweep example first establishes the serial mathematical reference.
lessons.pitfall: Changing the keyword from for to parfor does not remove a true dependency between iterations.

question.prompt: Which task is naturally independent across iterations?

options.text: One time recurrence reading the previous iteration’s state
Simulations with separate parameters and separate output slots

question.explanation: Independent trials can execute in any order without changing each trial’s inputs.

lessons.title: Data movement and GPU arrays
paragraphs: A GPU array places data in device memory so supported operations can run on the accelerator. Transferring data to and from the device has a cost. Large batches of suitable numerical work can amortize transfers; small operations interrupted by frequent gather calls may spend more time moving data than computing it.

Desktop gpuArray and gather require supported hardware and the relevant MATLAB product. Check function support, data precision and available device memory. Compare a CPU reference with GPU output using an appropriate tolerance. A browser plot of a scaling model is not evidence that a GPU executed the workload; this sandbox explicitly performs no GPU computation.
lessons.pitfall: GPU availability alone does not guarantee an end-to-end speedup.

question.prompt: Why can frequent gather calls hurt GPU performance?

options.text: They transfer results back to the host repeatedly

question.explanation: Transfer and synchronization costs can dominate small device computations.

lessons.title: Amdahl’s law and modeled limits
paragraphs: If a fraction s of fixed-size work is serial and the remainder scales ideally over p workers, Amdahl’s model predicts speedup 1/(s+(1-s)/p). It assumes the same workload and omits additional overhead. As p grows, the ideal limit is 1/s when s is positive. This is an explanatory upper-bound model, not a hardware measurement.

For s=0.2 and p=4, ideal speedup is 2.5, not four. Scheduling, communication, memory contention and transfers can reduce actual speedup. Strong scaling holds total work fixed; weak scaling increases work with resources. State which experiment you measured so a throughput increase is not misreported as lower latency for a fixed problem.
lessons.pitfall: Never label Amdahl model predictions as observed multicore or GPU measurements.

question.explanation: The denominator is 0.2+0.8/4=0.4, whose reciprocal is 2.5.

lessons.title: Verification and fair parallel experiments
paragraphs: Compute a serial reference before parallelizing. Compare all task outputs, handle empty partitions and use tolerances for reordered floating-point reductions. Set up independent random streams if tasks sample randomness. Race conditions and duplicated streams can produce superficially plausible results while violating the intended experiment.

Measure end-to-end and kernel-only scopes separately when that distinction is useful. Include pool startup if it belongs to the user-visible workload; report amortized repeated-run performance separately. Record workers, hardware, MATLAB version, data sizes and transfers. Desktop toolbox scripts in this course need local execution; no timing numbers are supplied as if they had been measured.
lessons.pitfall: A parallel result that merely has the expected shape still needs numerical comparison with its reference.

courses.title: 17. Images, symbolic math and the toolbox ecosystem
courses.summary: Connect core array skills to imaging, symbolic derivation, machine learning and external workflows without confusing them with browser capabilities.

lessons.title: Images as arrays
paragraphs: A grayscale image is a two-dimensional intensity array; a color image commonly has a third channel dimension. Its type and range matter: uint8 values often represent 0 through 255, while normalized floating-point images often use 0 through 1. A threshold comparison produces a logical segmentation mask, but the threshold alone does not establish what objects are present.

The browser exercise uses a small real matrix as a synthetic intensity image and computes a bright-pixel mask. Desktop imread and image display tools connect arrays to actual image files; Image Processing Toolbox adds operations such as morphology and region measurement. This lesson does not add camera acquisition or a trained vision model to the sandbox.
lessons.pitfall: Applying a threshold chosen for [0,1] data to raw [0,255] values changes the result dramatically.

question.prompt: Why must an image threshold specify its intensity range?

options.text: Because every image is binary already
Because plots choose the threshold automatically
The same numeric threshold has different meaning on different scales

question.explanation: Data type and normalization determine how a threshold relates to brightness.

lessons.title: Symbolic versus numerical mathematics
paragraphs: Symbolic expressions represent algebraic objects and can produce exact derivatives or simplifications. Numeric arrays store finite approximations and evaluate concrete values. In desktop Symbolic Math Toolbox, syms creates symbolic variables, diff differentiates an expression and subs substitutes values. This differs from numeric diff, which computes neighboring sample differences.

Use a symbolic derivation to obtain an analytical reference, then evaluate and test a numeric implementation on representative values. Symbolic success does not validate a physical assumption, and converting expressions to floating-point numbers reintroduces rounding. The browser has no symbolic engine; it teaches the distinction and provides a separately labelled desktop example.
lessons.pitfall: The same function name can dispatch differently for symbolic objects and numeric arrays.

options.text: An exact symbolic derivative of an arbitrary formula

question.explanation: The browser’s numeric diff operates on stored samples, unlike symbolic differentiation.

lessons.title: Machine learning and scientific workflows
paragraphs: A supervised learning workflow separates features from target labels, trains on one partition and evaluates on another. Scaling and feature selection must be fitted without leaking held-out information. Desktop Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox provides many estimators; Deep Learning Toolbox supplies neural-network tools. Product names do not eliminate the need for a sound evaluation design.

Begin with a simple baseline and a metric matched to the task. An imbalanced classifier can have high accuracy while missing nearly every rare event, so inspect errors by class. A regression benchmark should report prediction error in useful units. The browser’s polynomial and threshold exercises compute explicit models, not pretrained inference or a full training framework.
lessons.pitfall: Training accuracy alone is not evidence of performance on future data.

question.prompt: Why keep evaluation data separate from fitting decisions?

options.text: To reduce leakage and test generalization
To make training error exactly zero

question.explanation: Held-out observations should challenge decisions that were made without using their answers.

lessons.title: Navigating functions and product boundaries
paragraphs: MATLAB’s function ecosystem spans core language, numerical libraries and optional products. Read the function page’s syntax, input types, output conventions and product requirements. A name in this course reference is not a promise that every overload is supported in the browser. Each executable browser signature is listed explicitly; all other entries are desktop guidance.

Use the complete MathWorks function catalog to discover additional APIs. Verify availability with your installed products and release, then build a minimal self-contained example before integrating it into a larger project. File IO, tables, symbolic objects, optimizers, parallel workers and Simulink need their actual desktop capabilities; the sandbox never silently substitutes unrelated behavior.

courses.title: 18. Capstone: a tested thermal simulation
courses.summary: Combine array programming, simulation, numerical validation, parameter studies and clear reporting in one reproducible engineering investigation.

lessons.title: Model and dimensional contract
paragraphs: A lumped thermal model balances stored heat, input power and heat loss. Let C be heat capacity in joules per kelvin, G thermal conductance in watts per kelvin, P input power in watts and Ta ambient temperature. The rate law is dT/dt=(P-G*(T-Ta))/C. Constant parameters and uniform object temperature are modeling assumptions, not universal facts.

The equilibrium is Ta+P/G and the time constant is C/G. For C=20, G=2, P=10 and Ta=20, equilibrium is 25 degrees Celsius and tau=10 seconds. A Celsius temperature difference has the same magnitude as a kelvin difference in this balance. Require C>0 and G>0 before using those formulas.
lessons.pitfall: A single lumped state cannot represent arbitrary spatial temperature gradients.

question.prompt: For C=20 and G=2, what is the time constant?
question.explanation: The ratio C/G has units of seconds and equals 10.

lessons.title: Implement and verify the trajectory
paragraphs: Initialize T to ambient, construct a uniform time vector and preallocate the state array. At every step compute the heat-balance rate from the old state, then perform one Euler update. Keep parameters near the top of the script and use names that expose units. The independent constant-input solution is Ta+(P/G)*(1-exp(-t/tau)) for this initial condition.

Check the initial state, the maximum trajectory error and the long-time approach to equilibrium. At the default step h=0.5 seconds, the maximum absolute error should remain below 0.05 degrees. A changed parameter requires reevaluating the time step and expected results; assertions should follow the model contract rather than freeze every output to the original example.
lessons.pitfall: Updating the state before computing its own old-state rate can change the intended recurrence.

question.prompt: Which curve is an independent reference for the constant-input case?

options.text: The same Euler loop copied twice

question.explanation: The analytical solution follows from the linear rate law and initial condition.

lessons.title: Parameter studies and numerical evidence
paragraphs: Study one parameter at a time before combining changes. Increasing C slows the response without changing equilibrium when G and P stay fixed. Increasing G lowers equilibrium rise and reduces the time constant. Increasing P changes the equilibrium rise but not tau in this linear model. These predictions help detect swapped parameters or unit mistakes.

Repeat the same physical scenario at three time steps and record maximum error. Then sweep independent parameter values using separate runs or a loop, preserving each result. The trials are candidates for desktop parallel execution, but their state trajectories still depend on previous time steps. Distinguish parallel trials from incorrectly parallelizing a recurrence.
lessons.pitfall: A parameter sweep and time integration have different dependency structures.

question.prompt: What happens when C doubles with G and P fixed?

options.text: The time constant doubles and equilibrium stays the same
Equilibrium doubles and the time constant stays fixed

question.explanation: C affects stored energy and response speed; steady heat balance does not depend on C.

lessons.title: An engineering report and its limits
paragraphs: A complete report states the question, equations, units, assumptions, inputs, methods, checks, results and limitations. Include a plot with units, an error table and the exact script. Explain whether data are synthetic or measured. A simulation validated against its own analytical model is numerically verified; it is not experimentally validated against a real object.

Export the notebook for continued work, the .m script for MATLAB and computed results for review. Desktop extensions can use ode45, parameter estimation and independent parallel trials. Each extension needs its own correctness and environment checks. Passing the course exam records local study progress only; it does not certify the physical design or generate campaign XP.
lessons.pitfall: Numerical agreement with an equation does not prove the equation describes a particular device.
